extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent attorneys, and judges
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and defenses governing the sufficiency of patent specifications, novelty/prior-publication defenses, procedural notice requirements, and the statutory mechanisms (disclaimer, section 6) affecting validity and remedies in infringement suits. Focuses on what a specification must contain and how defendants may challenge a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description — distinguish from prior things
rubrics_metrics.description: "the inventor shall deliver a written description of his invention, 'in such full, clear, and exact terms, as to distinguish the same from all other things before known; and in the case of any machine, he shall fully explain the principle, and the several modes, in which he has contemplated the application of that principle, or character, by which it may be distinguished from other inventions.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must state in full and exact terms what the invention consists of so it can be determined whether it ought to be patented and whether the public infringe. If the description mixes old and new and does not distinctly ascertain what is new, the patent may be broader than the invention and thus void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement — must teach a skilled person to make and use
rubrics_metrics.description: "to enable any person skilled in the art or science, of which it is a branch, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make, compound, and use the same."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification need not instruct a layperson, but must be "in such full, clear, and exact terms" that a person skilled in the relevant art could construct and use the invention. The question is one of fact (and law on construction of the patent terms). A materially defective specification that prevents a skilled workman from making the machine is a good defence to an infringement action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must distinguish new from old (identify improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: "if it be an improvement only upon an existing machine, he should distinguish what is new and what is old in his specification"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee may not claim exclusive use of machinery already known. If the description mixes up old and new without clearly indicating what is claimed as new, the patent is void for covering too much or leaving uncertainty about what is claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defective, obscure, or ambiguous specification as a defence
rubrics_metrics.description: "if the specification be materially defective, or obscurely or so loosely worded, that a skilful workman in that particular art could not construct the machine, it is a good defence against the action"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under common law this could bar recovery even absent fraudulent intent. In U.S. statutory context, failure of statutory pre-requisites (like correct specification) may be shown as a defense in an infringement action; whether it voids the patent may depend on the statute and required procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment or addition must be for purpose of deceiving to void patent (§6)
rubrics_metrics.description: "the statute ... does not avoid the patent in such case, unless the 'concealment or addition shall fully appear to have been made for the purpose of deceiving the public.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defendant who seeks not merely to defend himself but to have the patent declared void under the statute must proceed under the statutory provision (section 6) and the jury must find the fraudulent intent to deceive the public. Without that finding, concealment/addition may be a defence to that suit but will not automatically invalidate the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between defense to infringement and action to annul patent
rubrics_metrics.description: "If the party is content with defending himself, he may either plead specially, or plead the general issue ... But if, not content with defending himself, he seeks to annul the patent, he must proceed in precise conformity to the sixth section."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defendant may obtain a verdict in his favor by showing pre-requisite failures, but to obtain a judgment declaring the patent void he must follow the statutory steps (including notice requirements) and obtain the requisite finding of intent where the statute demands it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / prior knowledge/public work defense
rubrics_metrics.description: "that the patentee was not the original and first inventor or discoverer of the thing patented, or of a substantial and material part thereof, claimed as new; or that it had been described in some public work, anterior to the supposed discovery thereof by the patentee."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To rely on lack of novelty, the defendant must show prior knowledge, use, or description in a public work before the patentee's discovery. Plaintiffs' rights relate back to the original discovery which may be proved by parol. This defense can render the patent void pro tanto for the part that lacks novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict notice and particularity requirements when alleging prior use/knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: "the same section of the statute requires that the defendant 'shall state, in his notice of special matter, the names and places of residence of those whom he intends to prove to have possessed a prior knowledge of the thing, and where the same had been used.' This provision must be strictly complied with."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting up the prior-knowledge/novelty defense, the defendant must strictly follow statutory notice requirements, giving names, residences, and locations of prior use; failure to comply can preclude the defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice must describe what part is charged with lack of novelty and source publications
rubrics_metrics.description: "the notice must describe whether the whole, or a part, and what part of the invention is to be charged with want of novelty, and in what public work or works, the whole, or a part, or what part had been described before the supposed discovery by the patentee."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid surprise and permit proper adjudication, the defendant's notice should specify the scope (whole or part) of the invention challenged and identify the prior publications or works relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of foreign prior use/publication and the 1836 proviso
rubrics_metrics.description: "whenever it shall satisfactorily appear that the patentee, at the time of making his application for the patent, believed himself to be the first inventor ... the same shall not be held to be void, on account of the invention or discovery ... having been before known or used in any foreign country, it not appearing that the same or any substantial part of thereof had before been patented or described in any printed publication;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely showing prior knowledge/use abroad does not necessarily defeat a U.S. patent if the patentee honestly believed he was first and there was no prior patent or printed publication describing the invention. The proviso limits the reach of foreign prior-use evidence unless it was publicly documented (printed publication/patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer procedure to remove erroneously claimed parts (Act of 1837)
rubrics_metrics.description: "any such patentee ... may make disclaimer of such parts of the thing patented, as the disclaimant shall not claim to hold by virtue of the patent ... which disclaimer shall thereafter be taken and considered as part of the original specification ... recorded in the patent office ... On payment ... of the sum of ten dollars."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee who inadvertently claimed more than he had the right to claim may file a written, witnessed disclaimer recorded in the patent office (fee required). To obtain benefits (e.g., costs) in pending suits the disclaimer must be filed before suit commencement; unreasonable delay in filing can be a defense to the suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'description' for prior-publication purposes — must enable practice
rubrics_metrics.description: "the description must be such as to give the public the means of knowledge, or, in other words, must of itself enable the public to practise the invention ... mere speculations or suggestions ... not stated in such a way as to serve for a practical direction ... are ... not held to have defeated the patents."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a prior printed description to defeat a later patent it must approach the character of a specification and serve as a practical direction for making or practicing the invention. Mere hints, speculative suggestions, or non-practical experimental notes are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public accessibility determines effect of prior printed description
rubrics_metrics.description: "the intention of Congress was, to make it a conclusive presumption that the patentee had seen any printed description of the thing, which had been so printed and published as to be accessible to the public ... not ... in cases ... published and circulated in such a manner as not to be accessible either to the public or to him."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a printed description operates as prior art depends on whether it was published in a way accessible to the public; this is a jury question considering the circumstances of publication. Private or narrowly circulated printed items may not be treated as public works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior description must supply means of knowledge without further invention
rubrics_metrics.description: "unless the description would enable the public, without further invention to put the thing in practice, it cannot be said that a knowledge of that thing is in the possession of the public."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior description defeats a subsequent patent only if it provides sufficient information so the public could practice the invention without performing further inventive work. It need not show reduction to practice, but must give practical instructions.
